At 4:17 every morning, the city briefly remembers that it was once a marsh.

The gutters shine. Mist gathers above the roads. In the pale silence before delivery trucks and school buses, the buildings seem less permanent—just tall reeds with lit windows, leaning together for warmth. Somewhere beneath the asphalt, water moves through forgotten channels, carrying leaves, coins, and the small metallic secrets of the year.

Mara knows this because she walks then.

She leaves her apartment without turning on the lights. The cat watches from the windowsill, offended by her departure but unwilling to admit concern. Outside, the air tastes of rain and stone. She passes the bakery, where tomorrow’s bread is already becoming today’s smell, and the laundromat, whose fluorescent lights hum like a tired insect.

At the corner is the old tree.

No one knows what kind it is. Its trunk has split around a rusted bicycle rack, and its roots have lifted the sidewalk into a series of uneven steps. Every spring, despite the salt and exhaust and the absence of anything resembling permission, it produces white flowers.

Mara stops beneath it.

One flower has fallen into a puddle. The reflection trembles whenever a car passes, so the flower appears to bloom and vanish, bloom and vanish.

She thinks of all the things people call permanent: addresses, promises, names carved into benches. She thinks of how quickly the world revises itself. A storefront becomes a café, the café becomes a clinic, the clinic becomes an empty room with dust gathering in the corners. Friends move away. Parents become photographs. Even grief, given enough mornings, develops a routine.

Still, the tree flowers.

This is not a lesson. It does not explain anything. The tree is not brave. It has no opinion about survival. It simply receives what arrives—rain, winter, pruning, pigeons—and makes, when it can, a little brightness.

Mara reaches up and touches one of the branches.

From somewhere far off, a train begins to move. The sound travels through the ground before it reaches the air. The city stirs above the old marsh, unaware of its roots.

By five o’clock, the streets will fill.

For now, there is only the wet pavement, the pale sky, and one white flower trembling in the dark water.
